common_name: Silver Umbrella Japanese Angelica Tree (Fine-Margined Variegated Devil's Walking Stick)

planting.note: Plant grafted container specimens in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sited out of strong wind, which can tatter the broad leaflets and scorch the fine white leaf margins.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun and wind, both of which can scorch the leaf margins. 'Silver Umbrella' carries the same huge, twice-compound, spine-stemmed architecture as the species, but each leaflet is edged in a finer, more refined white margin than the more common 'Variegata', giving the whole tiered leaf a lighter, lacier appearance, and the plant typically stays somewhat more modest in ultimate size. Massive creamy-white flower panicles appear in late summer above the foliage. It suckers less vigorously than the green-leaved species, and reverted all-green shoots should be pruned out promptly at the base to preserve the variegation. Propagation is by grafting, since seedlings do not come true.

common_name: Golden Umbrella Japanese Angelica Tree (Gold-Margined Variegated Devil's Walking Stick)

planting.note: Plant grafted container specimens in spring in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, sited out of strong wind, which can tatter the broad leaflets and scorch the gold leaf margins.

directions: Plant in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun and wind, both of which can scorch the gold leaf margins. A rare, newer selection than the classic 'Aureovariegata', 'Golden Umbrella' unfurls deep green in spring and gradually develops broad gold margins that fade toward white as the season progresses, layered on the same tiered, horizontally held, twice-compound foliage typical of the species. Huge, erect panicles of small creamy-white flowers appear from late summer, followed by non-edible purple-black berries, and foliage often turns fiery orange and burgundy before falling in autumn. It suckers less vigorously than the green-leaved species, and reverted all-green shoots should be pruned out promptly at the base to preserve the variegation. Propagation is by grafting, since seedlings do not come true.

common_name: Jagged Edge Leopard Plant (Large-Clumping Toothed-Leaf Farfugium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in consistently moist, rich soil in part sun to light shade after the last frost.

directions: A selection from Japan's Kairyoen Nursery grown by Juniper Level Botanic Garden/Plant Delights Nursery since 2003, 'Jagged Edge' forms one of the largest clumps of any named farfugium selection, with bold, glossy, round green leaves up to a foot wide edged in a distinctive jagged, toothed margin. Grow it in part sun to light shade in evenly moist, humus-rich soil, where it spreads into an imposing 4 to 5 foot wide specimen clump useful as a bold accent or groundcover under high shade. In late October it sends up 3-foot spikes of bright yellow daisy flowers well above the foliage, giving a stronger floral display than most foliage-focused farfugium cultivars.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden — Farfugium japonicum 'Jagged Edge'

common_name: Purple Cloak Alocasia (Purple-Backed Velvet Elephant Ear)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants after all frost danger has passed, in rich, well-drained but moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; protect from direct sun, which can scorch the sandpapery leaves.

directions: Plant in rich, well-drained, consistently moist soil in bright, filtered shade; 'Purple Cloak' is a rare Bornean selection of Alocasia princeps grown for its V-shaped, sandpapery-textured leaves with a glossy dark green-blue-silver upper surface and a striking deep purple-red underside carried on plum-purple petioles. Long internodes between leaves keep the upper growth open and architectural rather than dense, and the plant stays relatively compact, usually under 4 feet tall, making it well suited to a large container or a sheltered shade bed. Keep soil evenly moist but never waterlogged, since Alocasia are prone to rot in soggy conditions, and where winters bring frost, grow it as a container specimen brought indoors or dig and store the rhizome like a dahlia tuber.
